input:
This worked example walks through the determination of the
available net positive suction head for a pump drawing condensate
from an open tank, the quantity that decides whether the pump can
draw at its duty flow without cavitation. Because the tank is open,
the pressure at the surface of the liquid is the atmospheric
pressure $P_{atm}$, 101.3 kPa. Set against this is the vapour
pressure $P_v$ of the condensate at the pumping temperature,
7.4 kPa. Two further quantities complete the picture: the static
lift $h_{lift}$, 3.7 m, and the friction loss $h_f$ in the suction
line, 0.8 m. The available net positive suction head is computed
from these quantities by the relation

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

in which $\rho$ stands for the density of the condensate and $g$
for gravitational acceleration. The first term represents the
pressure head standing above vapour pressure at the tank surface,
expressed as a height of the liquid itself, while the static lift
and the friction loss are subtracted because both are heads the
liquid must supply before it reaches the pump inlet. Substituting
the values gives the result $NPSH_a$ = 5.1 m.

It remains to be emphasised that the computed head, 5.1 m, is a
margin to be tested rather than a result to be filed away. The
pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve,
and the available head of 5.1 m must be shown to exceed that
required value with a proper margin; should it fall short, the
pump will cavitate at the duty flow.

The tank is open, so the pressure at the liquid surface is the

suction line is 0.8 m. The available net positive suction head is
computed from these quantities by

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $\rho$ denotes the density of the condensate and $g$ denotes

standing above vapour pressure at the tank surface, expressed as a

The computed head is a margin to be tested, not a result to be
